evidence.claim: A desert drive follows the railroad grade past abandoned townsites.
evidence.quote: Traversing the flatlands of the Great Salt Lake Desert

evidence.claim: The Transcontinental Railroad Back Country Byway follows the old Central Pacific grade across the flatlands of the Great Salt Lake Desert.
evidence.quote: Traversing the flatlands of the Great Salt Lake Desert, the byway stretches between the area just west of Golden Spike National Historic Site and the Utah-Nevada border, following the deserted Central Pacific Railroad grade lain in 1869.

evidence.claim: The Bureau of Land Management allows three to four hours for the 90-mile drive.
evidence.quote: Allow 3-4 hours to drive this 90 mile stretch.

evidence.claim: Managed as a National Backcountry Byway, it passes ghost towns, foundations, earthworks and culverts that BLM identifies as remnants of the railroad.
evidence.quote: 90 miles of original hand-constructed Transcontinental Railroad grade, managed as a National Backcountry Byway and located west of the Golden Spike National Historic Park. Visitors will pass through ghost towns and see old foundations, earthworks, culverts, and trestles

evidence.claim: Expect rough roads in a remote setting.
evidence.quote: be prepared for rough roads in a remote setting.

evidence.claim: The grade dates to 1869.
evidence.quote: following the deserted Central Pacific Railroad grade lain in 1869.

evidence.claim: Central Pacific had built east from Sacramento while Union Pacific worked west from Omaha, with thousands of workers, mostly of Chinese, Irish or Mormon descent, employed by the two companies.
evidence.quote: the Union Pacific Railroad who started building west from Omaha, Nebraska, and the Central Pacific Railroad who started building east from Sacramento, California. Both companies required the hiring of thousands of workers, mostly of Chinese, Irish, or Mormon descent.

evidence.claim: In 1904, Southern Pacific completed the Lucin Cutoff across the Great Salt Lake, bypassing Terrace and reducing its tracks to a little-used branch line.
evidence.quote: In 1904 the Southern Pacific Railroad, successor to the Central Pacific, completed the Lucin Cutoff across the Great Salt Lake. The new route bypassed Terrace, and the tracks through town became a little-used branchline.

evidence.claim: The rails came up in 1942; BLM designated the grade as part of the byway in 1993.
evidence.quote: The tracks along the grade were removed in 1942. The grade was added to the National Register of Historic Places in 1987, as part of the Central Pacific Railroad Grade Historic District. In 1993 the Bureau of Land Management designated the grade as part of the  Transcontinental Railroad Back Country Byway.

evidence.claim: Traveling from the Utah-Nevada border toward the area west of Golden Spike follows the former railroad corridor.
evidence.quote: the byway stretches between the area just west of Golden Spike National Historic Site and the Utah-Nevada border, following the deserted Central Pacific Railroad grade

evidence.claim: At Terrace, a turntable outline survives beside the old railroad bed.
evidence.quote: only a pile of red bricks and the outline of the turntable is next to the old railroad bed.

evidence.claim: Next comes Matlin, with the profile of a rail wye, then Kelton, where abandoned foundations and a cemetery remain.
evidence.quote: All that is left of the town is the profile in the rail grade of a wye built in 1900.

evidence.claim: Next comes Matlin, with the profile of a rail wye, then Kelton, where abandoned foundations and a cemetery remain.
evidence.quote: Nothing remains but some ruins, fallen buildings and abandoned foundations, and a deteriorating cemetery.

evidence.claim: Beyond is Kosmo, with concrete foundations and canals in its western section.
evidence.quote: All that remain of the town are a few concrete foundations and canals in West Kosmo.

evidence.claim: A turntable outline and a pile of red bricks mark Terrace beside the old railroad bed.
evidence.quote: only a pile of red bricks and the outline of the turntable is next to the old railroad bed.

evidence.claim: Established in 1869 as a Central Pacific operations base, the town had a 16-stall roundhouse and an eight-track switchyard.
evidence.quote: The town was established April 1, 1869, as a Central Pacific Railroad "division point" (operations base), on the route of the First transcontinental railroad and included a 16-stall roundhouse and an eight-track switchyard.

evidence.claim: The Lucin Cutoff bypassed it in 1904.
evidence.quote: In 1904 the Southern Pacific Railroad, successor to the Central Pacific, completed the Lucin Cutoff across the Great Salt Lake. The new route bypassed Terrace

evidence.claim: The railroad closed its facilities and transferred the division point to Montello, Nevada; many houses and buildings followed.
evidence.quote: The railroad closed its facilities at Terrace, moving the division point to Montello, Nevada, about 40 miles (64 km) to the west–southwest. The railroad line through Terrace was finally abandoned in 1942. Many of Terrace's houses and buildings were moved to Montello.

evidence.claim: The line was abandoned in 1942, and the surviving cemetery has only three headstones.
evidence.quote: The railroad line through Terrace was finally abandoned in 1942. Many of Terrace's houses and buildings were moved to Montello. The cemetery still remains with only three headstones

evidence.claim: The town and nearby Terrace Mountain took their names from shoreline terraces left by the former Lake Bonneville in this area.
evidence.quote: The former town (as well as the nearby Terrace Mountain) was named for the shoreline terraces of the former Lake Bonneville in the area.

evidence.claim: There are no facilities or services along the byway. BLM advises carrying water and spare tires; flat tires are common.
evidence.quote: There are no facilities or services available along the backcountry byway.

evidence.claim: There are no facilities or services along the byway. BLM advises carrying water and spare tires; flat tires are common.
evidence.quote: Visitors should carry plenty of water, spare tires, and be prepared for rough roads in a remote setting. Flat tires are common along the byway; visitors should be knowledgeable on how to change a tire.

evidence.claim: Matlin survives as the profile of a wye built into the railroad grade in 1900.
evidence.quote: All that is left of the town is the profile in the rail grade of a wye built in 1900.

evidence.claim: Chinese railroad workers built the small community and its track-support facilities. Central Pacific Railroad established the town on April 5, 1869.
evidence.quote: The former town was established by the Central Pacific Railroad (CPRR) on April 5, 1869. Chinese railroad workers built a small community and facilities to support the track section.

evidence.claim: Its recorded population was 15 in 1870 and 25 in 1876, figures that most likely excluded Chinese residents.
evidence.quote: Records indicate that the population was 15 people in 1870 and 25 in 1876. These numbers most likely did not include Chinese residents.

evidence.claim: It depended on the railroad throughout its history and was abandoned when the Lucin Cutoff was finished in 1904.
evidence.quote: The town relied on the railroad through its entire history. In 1904 the site was abandoned when the Lucin Cutoff was finished.

evidence.claim: A lightning-caused wildfire in June 2020 damaged or destroyed many artifacts that had remained at the site.
evidence.quote: In June 2020, the Matlin Fire (a lightning caused wildfire, which started June 4) eventually burned about 8,000 acres (3,200 ha) in the area surrounding Matlin. The fire damaged some, and destroyed many other, significant artifacts that had previously remained at the site.

evidence.claim: Kelton connected the railroad with a stagecoach route to Boise by the summer of 1869.
evidence.quote: Already by the summer of 1869 a stagecoach route was established between Kelton and Boise, Idaho.

evidence.claim: That route was defunct by July 1884 as other railroads reached northern markets.
evidence.quote: The importance of the freight road waned as the Oregon Short Line Railroad and the Utah Northern Railroad pushed into Oregon, Idaho, and Montana. By July 1884 the stage route was defunct

evidence.claim: The Lucin Cutoff later left Kelton on a backup line serving local farmers and ranchers.
evidence.quote: Kelton's former section was relegated to a mere backup line, used in case of high water, and to service local farmers and ranchers.

evidence.claim: The 1934 earthquake had already damaged the schoolhouse so severely that it had to be abandoned, though the town itself survived.
evidence.quote: On the morning of March 12, 1934, Kelton was hit by the most powerful earthquake ever recorded in Utah.

evidence.claim: The 1934 earthquake had already damaged the schoolhouse so severely that it had to be abandoned, though the town itself survived.
evidence.quote: the Kelton schoolhouse was left leaning at such a precarious angle that it had to be abandoned.

evidence.claim: Even in 1937, it remained a local shipping point with 47 residents.
evidence.quote: As late as 1937 Kelton was still an important local shipping point, and a population of 47 remained.

evidence.claim: The rails were dismantled in 1942, and the last residents departed, taking some houses with them.
evidence.quote: Southern Pacific Railroad completely dismantled the old railway line in a week, July 1–8, 1942, and contributed the hardware to the war effort. The last residents of Kelton left, taking some of the houses with them.

evidence.claim: Foundations, fallen buildings and a cemetery remain.
evidence.quote: Nothing remains but some ruins, fallen buildings and abandoned foundations, and a deteriorating cemetery.
